comment: Ecosystem-tool arms (the second arm class). Every entry is a tool a user would reach for, listed with the exact argv the runner executes - no shell, no string interpolation beyond {input} and {script_dir}. Reports produced from here carry arm_class=tool and are never rendered in the same table as a parity arm (ROADMAP 7.1). A tool is added only after its argv has been verified against the installed version and recorded here.

pyfastx-stat.notes: The CLI subcommand is `stat`, not `stats` (checked against pyfastx 2.3.1 with `pyfastx --help`); it prints per-file statistics to stdout.

r-prcomp.notes: The R parity arm deliberately hand-writes its power iteration; this arm is the call a user would actually make. Both read the same matrix file, so the difference is the implementation, not the input handling.

py-sklearn-pca.notes: The Python parity arm hand-writes the power iteration with stdlib only; this arm is the import a user would actually make. `python3` must be the interpreter that has scikit-learn installed (the pack venv on the measurement host), which the report's version string makes checkable.

seqkit-stats.notes: The streaming reference for sequence.stats: seqkit stats reports num_seqs/sum_len/min_len/avg_len/max_len/N50 for FASTA/Q in a single streaming pass, which is the same job our capability does with a record-oriented parser. Subcommand spelling checked against seqkit v2.14.0 with `seqkit stats --help` (it is `stats`, not `stat`); the binary was verified byte-for-byte against the publisher's GitHub API asset digest sha256:3d664ffb48438d1fbd3f3cfc060c71d00368a26435f1c876944aea7fcdff86b5 before install, so this arm answers whether our implementation is slow or whether streaming FASTA statistics are intrinsically slow.
